abstract: Abstract This study examines the impact of Buddhist Jataka tales, rich in compassion, kindness, and selflessness on fostering empathy in children. abstract: We investigate whether Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit altruistic tendencies, and critically, whether their implicit associations and self-reports predict actual altruistic behavior. Using a multi-method approach inspired by human social psychology, we tested 24 frontier LLMs across three paradigms: (1) an Implicit Association Test (IAT) measuring implicit altruism bias, (2) a forced binary choice task measuring behavioral altruism, and (3) a self-assessment scale measuring explicit altruism beliefs. Our key findings are: (1) All models show strong implicit pro-altruism bias (mean IAT = 0.87, p < .0001), confirming models "know" altruism is good. (2) Models behave more altruistically than chance (65.6% vs. 50%, p < .0001), but with substantial variation (48-85%). (3) Implicit associations do not predict behavior (r = .22, p = .29). (4) Most critically, models systematically overestimate their own altruism, claiming 77.5% altruism while acting at 65.6% (p < .0001, Cohen's d = 1.08). This "virtue signaling gap" affects 75% of models tested. Based on these findings, we recommend the Calibration Gap (the discrepancy between self-reported and behavioral values) as a standardized alignment metric. Well-calibrated models are more predictable and behaviorally consistent; only 12.5% of models achieve the ideal combination of high prosocial behavior and accurate self-knowledge.

abstract: Music has existed in human culture for at least 40,000 years and is present today in all societies. Its perception, appreciation and production are based on a set of cognitive abilities commonly referred to as "musicality." Some authors have suggested that musicality may have an evolutionary origin. Specifically, it may have evolved because music promotes social cohesion within groups. This hypothesis is supported by studies in developmental psychology, which show that joint music-making promotes empathy in 8 to 11-year-olds, as well as cooperation and helping behavior in 4-year-old children. However, many questions remain unanswered, particularly regarding the effects of music listening on social behavior (beyond joint production), the conditions under which such effects may be observed (e.g., individual versus joint listening), the musical properties and mechanisms involved (e.g., the role of rhythm and interpersonal synchronization), and the broader evolution of musicality across the living world beyond our own species. In 2017, we already demonstrated a positive influence of joint listening to classical music on social interaction in a cooperative task context in children aged 3 to 6, as well as in a parrot species, the cockatiels (suggesting convergent evolution in humans and certain birds, thus indicating a partly biological, not just cultural, origin of musicality). The study presented here focuses specifically on children but is also part of a larger comparative project involving humans, non-human primates, and birds. In the case of children, this study showed that percussive, rhythmic electronic music fostered more social interactions and cooperation among pairs of 3 to 6-year-old children compared to classical music (Mozart's Sonata K448), white noise, a "scrambled" version of the stimulus used, or silence. The role of rhythm and interpersonal synchronization will be further explored in the future by testing the influence of new stimuli listened to together or separately, with or without concurrent music production. We also plan to examine the spontaneous movements of individuals during listening and their relationship to observed behaviors in subsequent prosocial tasks.

abstract: There is growing interest in the effects of reading on empathy and prosocial behaviour but not enough is known about the associations among these variables in children. In a study undertaken at a single time point, we examined children's leisure reading and self-reported prosocial behaviour, and whether the relation between them was mediated by affective or cognitive empathy or by theory of mind. abstract: The Enterobacteriaceae family, which includes prominent pathogens such as K. pneumoniae, E. coli, and S. enterica, poses a significant global health threat due to the rapid dissemination of multidrug resistance and virulence determinants. Central to this dissemination are conjugative plasmids, which act as vehicles for horizontal gene transfer. Among the myriad defense systems that interact with these mobile genetic elements, the type IV-A CRISPR-Cas system stands out due to its enigmatic nature and unique plasmid-centric biology. Unlike canonical CRISPR-Cas systems that are chromosomal and target bacteriophages, type IV-A systems are predominantly encoded on large, conjugative plasmids, particularly those bearing IncHI1B/IncFIB replicons. This review synthesizes current evidence on the biology of type IV-A systems within Enterobacteriaceae, elucidating their role as mediators of inter-plasmid competition, their paradoxical association with the spread of antibiotic resistance and virulence genes, and their emerging applications as programmable tools. We explore the mechanistic basis for their function as a natural CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) system, the epidemiological landscape of their distribution, and the dual role they play in both constraining and facilitating the dissemination of clinically relevant traits. Finally, we propose ambitious research avenues, including the development of "plasmid-destroying" probiotics, the use of type IV-A systems as epidemiological biosensors, and the exploration of hypotheses concerning their role in mediating bacterial "altruism" or serving as a "genetic memory" of the plasmid "secretoome."

abstract: Punishment conveys social information to transgressors, who attribute motives to punishers. Drawing on the motive-attribution framework, we examined whether transgressors' attributions to competitive (i.e. harming transgressors), individualistic (i.e. managing one's own interests) and prosocial (i.e. healing relationships) motives differ depending on whether punishment is administered by victims (second-party punishment) or uninvolved observers (third-party punishment), and how these attributions relate to downstream affective, relational and behavioural outcomes. In an incentivized Stealing Game, participants could steal valuable points and were punished either by the victim or an observer. Subsequently, transgressors reported their motive attributions, affect and willingness to reconcile and completed a measure of prosocial behaviour towards an unrelated other. Contrary to predictions, motive attributions did not systematically differ between second- and third-party punishment, except that third-party punishment was more strongly attributed to reputational concerns (i.e. a subdimension of individualistic motive attribution). Punishment severity emerged as an important predictor, with harsher sanctions linked to stronger competitive and individualistic attributions. Competitive motive attribution, in turn, was associated with higher negative affect and lower positive affect, willingness to reconcile and prosocial behaviour. Overall, transgressors' responses to punishment were less clearly shaped by who punished and more closely linked to punishment severity and motive attribution.

abstract: In contrast to the deficit-based approach, the double empathy problem (DEP) theory asserts that empathy functions bidirectionally, with interaction challenges stemming from differing expectations across individuals. This study aimed to examine how non-autistic individuals interpret the reactions of autistic and non-autistic children. We provided 61 non-autistic adult perceivers with 301 transcripts of speech substance from 82 autistic and non-autistic children, who answered questions evaluating cognitive empathy, affective empathy, and proposed responses across various emotional states. Adult perceivers rated children's responses on a scale of 1-5 (from lowest to highest) about the child's ability to understand emotions, empathize with those emotions, and suggest suitable prosocial responses. Their understanding of autism, autism-related traits, and previous interactions with autistic individuals were also examined. Our findings indicated adults assigned lower ratings to the empathetic responses of autistic children compared to those of non-autistic children. Individuals with a deeper understanding of autism, grounded in the medical paradigm, demonstrated a more pronounced disparity in their evaluations of autistic versus non-autistic responses. The studies indicate that autistic individuals may exhibit different empathy responses compared to their non-autistic counterparts, and these may be misinterpreted by non-autistic individuals, particularly by those who adhere to a deficit-based medical model.

abstract: Mosques play a vital role in Islam, serving not only as places of worship but also as centers for various social activities and economic empowerment, including the collection of social funds such as zakat, infaq, and sadaqah (charity). However, data from the 2024 Mosque Information System (SIMAS) of the Ministry of Religious Affairs of the Republic of Indonesia shows that of the total 694,725 mosques and prayer rooms, only 28,138 have a Mosque Welfare Agency (BKM), indicating that the majority of mosque management remains traditional and has not adopted modern management. Masjid Raya Al Insan (MRAI) in Kebayoran Lama, South Jakarta, is known for frequently holding social and humanitarian activities, both routine and incidental, for the congregation and the community living around the mosque. Previous research has examined factors such as transparency, accountability, the attitude of mosque management, and the social and religious influences of donors on trust and donation decisions. However, there is still little research that specifically examines the role of the effectiveness of mosque social activities and their consistency on repeat donation decisions. Using a qualitative case study method through in-depth interviews with administrators and donors, this study evaluates the role of the effectiveness and consistency of MRAI's social programs on repeat donations. The results show that the effectiveness of social activities is assessed by the emotional impact and tangible solutions for the community, not simply by statistical figures. It was found that repeat donation decisions are driven by a strong synergy between theological motivation and trust in the integrity of the administrators. Specifically, the consistency of social programs proved to be a key factor in building donor loyalty, validating the paradigm that "busy mosques" that actively distribute funds actually attract more donations. The study concluded that program consistency creates a sense of security and inner satisfaction for donors. As a recommendation, mosque administrators need to immediately undertake digital transformation in transparent financial reporting and implement Customer Relationship Management (CRM) to maintain donor relationships to ensure the sustainability of funding for community programs.

abstract: This study examines differential effects that different demographic variables and the subgroup-based community management model in universities on college students' prosocial behavior. Our dataset includes survey responses from 307 students enrolled in universities implementing this management model and 200 students from non-implementing universities. We employed the Random Forest algorithm to training AI model on 90% of the participant sample and reserving the remaining 10% for validation. The model achieved a prediction accuracy of 96.08%, demonstrating strong reliability in assessing the relationship between community-based subgroup management and prosocial behavioral outcomes. Furthermore, Random Forest shows the importance of independent variables.

abstract: Social norms shape a vast range of human behaviors, from everyday interactions to major life choices. Yet, existing theories of norm emergence typically focus either on why certain norms arise (substantive properties) or on how they spread and persist (dynamical properties), often making conflicting assumptions. Here, we propose a unified account in which norms prescribing how one ought to act emerge naturally from the fundamental algorithms that guide learning—whether in social or non-social settings. Our account builds on recent advances in decision-making and emotion research that have highlighted ‘actor-critic’ models as a core mechanism of learning from feedback. We extend this mechanism to social settings by assuming that it is not only we who critique our actions, others critique our actions as well. By simulating this interindividual form of learning, we show that it uniquely produces group behavior that exhibits both substantive and dynamical properties of real-world social norms, including prosociality, ingroup bias, stickiness, S-shaped curves, and local conformity / global diversity. Our framework thus offers a uniquely parsimonious way to bridge the gap between individual learning and group behavior.

abstract: The extent to which developmental science has mapped associations between cognitive, academic and socio-emotional functioning; caregiver reports and non-participant observation of young children was examined. Initially, 88 studies comprising over 300 effects were identified. The relationships between outcome measures and research design was described. Findings show that recurrent associations between task performance, behavioral report and naturalistic observation appear in this literature. The most frequently occurring comparisons in school settings were those between children’s disruptive-aggressive behavior, on-task/off-task behavior, prosocial behavior, externalizing problems, prosocial skills and early math and language achievement. In home settings, those between children’s positive/negative affect, engagement, compliance, temperament, cognitive and motor development were most common. Despite conceptual overlap, limited access to correlational data and between-study heterogeneity hinders cross-sample comparisons.

abstract: Sports events are leisure activities that contribute to public well-being. To maximize their benefits, large-scale improvements and the continuous accumulation of small, low-cost, and immediately actionable improvements are needed. However, systematic approaches for the improvement of safety and enjoyment in sports events remain limited. Hence, this study developed and evaluated the Sports Event Improvement for Safe, Move, Info, Link, and Environment (SMILE) program based on Participatory Action-Oriented Training (PAOT). The SMILE program was developed using a research and development framework and evaluated through field research and questionnaire. Field research covered professional football, basketball, and rugby games in Japan. The program involved 294 participants in Day 1 fieldwork and 243 in Day 2 workshops. Output evaluation assessed good practices, improvement proposals based on the program design principle of balancing safety and enjoyment, club feedback, and participant satisfaction. Outcome evaluation examined pre-post changes in engagement with sports clubs, spectating, supporting, and participating in sports, and PAOT. Participants collected 2,951 photographs of good practices and proposed 174 improvements. Output evaluation demonstrated high participant satisfaction and positive club feedback. Outcome evaluation showed significant pre-post increases in engagement with sports and PAOT. A 30-item action checklist based on photographs was developed to support the program. The SMILE program was developed as a participatory approach to the sustained improvement of safety and enjoyment in sports events. It promotes the refinement and sharing of good practices, the accumulation of small, low-cost, and immediately actionable improvements, and value co-creation among stakeholders.

abstract: Recent advances in moral decision-making research show people are hyperaltruistic by being more willing to sacrifice monetary gains to spare others from suffering than to spare themselves. Yet other studies indicate an opposite egoistic bias: subjects are less willing to harm themselves for others' benefits than for their own. These results underscore the complexities of moral decisions and demand a mechanistic explanation for hyperaltruistic preferences. We investigated hyperaltruism using trade-off choices combining monetary gains and painful electric shocks and choices combining monetary losses and shocks. Study 1 revealed that switching the decision context from gains to losses effectively eliminated the hyperaltruistic preference, accompanied by the altered relationship between subjects' instrumental harm (IH) trait attitudes and relative pain sensitivities. In the pre-registered study 2, we found that oxytocin, a neuropeptide linked to parochial altruism, restored the context-dependent hyperaltruistic preference. Furthermore, oxytocin increased the degree to which subjects framed the task as harming others, which mediated the correlation between IH and relative pain sensitivities. Thus, the loss decision context and oxytocin diminished and restored the mediation effect of subjective harm framing, respectively. Our results help elucidate the psychological processes underpinning the contextual specificity of hyperaltruism and carry implications in promoting prosocial interactions.

abstract: Abstract Symbolic promotions are an increasingly prevalent marketing practice globally, yet little is known about how or when they influence consumer behavior. We conceptualize symbolic promotions as a distinct type of sales promotion that creates value by reinforcing consumers' social identity through shared group membership rather than by providing economic incentives, such as reward-based promotions, or supporting distant others, such as cause-related marketing promotions (CMPs). We investigate the effectiveness of symbolic promotions and their underlying mechanisms using a multimethod approach. A nine-year longitudinal field study of daily sales for 22,084 books demonstrates that an existing symbolic promotion ("On August 12, I buy a Quebec book!") generates a substantial increase in sales, with stronger effects for lesser-known brands than for well-known brands. A follow-up experiment uncovers the unique mechanisms underlying these effects, showing that symbolic promotions stimulate curiosity and community rootedness, which in turn enhance multiple types of behavioral intentions, i.e., the likelihood of participating in the promotion, sharing it on social media, and future brand consideration. Together, these findings position symbolic promotions as a distinct, complementary addition to firms’ promotional portfolios, and demonstrate how firms can leverage shared identities to create value beyond traditional monetary incentives, with implications for various stakeholders.

abstract: Communication partners are crucial for adults with severe learning disabilities, as they recognise, interpret, and respond to verbal and non-verbal cues while sharing responsibility for creating a meaningful two-way communication process. Evidence-based strategies such as augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) can enhance interactions; however, their implementation in social care settings is inconsistent, constrained by workforce, organisational, and systemic barriers. This study-which forms part of the Improving Communication with Adults with Learning Disabilities (ICALD) programme-aimed to identify stakeholder-perceived barriers and facilitators to good communication support and to co-develop a Theory of Change (ToC) to guide implementation improvements in social care settings. Forty-eight stakeholders from diverse backgrounds, including adults with learning disabilities, participated in a total of 15 ToC workshops, one focus group, two interviews, and four supported conversations. Template Analysis based on the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) was used to identify core themes, barriers, and facilitators across CFIR domains. These key findings informed the iterative, collaborative development of the ToC map. Implementation barriers and facilitators identified across the CFIR domains indicated individual-, organisational-, and system-level factors influencing communication support. Key barriers included limited access to specialist professionals, inconsistent training, fragmented information-sharing systems, and variable staff knowledge of communication needs. Facilitators included strong leadership commitment, collaborative working with speech and language therapists and family carers, and peer mentoring. Supported conversations highlighted the importance of staff responsiveness to non-verbal cues. The resulting ToC map outlines short-, intermediate-, and long-term outcomes through three core pathways: (1) collaborative development of resources and training, (2) improved information sharing and recording, and (3) ongoing skills development, coaching, and supervision. Improving the implementation of good communication support for adults with severe learning disabilities is likely to depend on organisational commitment, leadership engagement, and structured workforce development supported by specialist input. The ToC developed provides a theoretically grounded framework for translating known facilitators into practical, context-specific strategies. It highlights the necessity of capacity-building within teams and organisational alignment with the communication rights of adults with severe learning disabilities to achieve sustainable, consistent and effective practice change.

abstract: Social media (SM) use has increased among adolescents, who are also more susceptible to the obesogenic digital food environment. One important nudge is 'Foodporn': sharing of alluring food images, a concept often associated with creating demand for unhealthy foods. However, this study assessed the use of foodporn images on SM as a possible visual stimulant to prime choices of healthy foods among adolescents. Also, assessed if secondary determinants associated with unhealthy food choices are relevant when promoting healthy foods using foodporn. A sequential explanatory mixed-methods design with an intervention framework was utilized. The quantitative phase involved 3 stages of online data collection using pretested questionnaires (N = 203). An item pool of 15 images categorized into 3 groups: "unhealthy foodporn" (unhealthy foods depicted in alluring pictures), "healthy foodporn" (healthy foods depicted in alluring pictures), and "healthy regular" (healthy foods depicted as regular pictures) was created and images were shared on Instagram for 15 days with a questionnaire assessing possible choices. The qualitative phase involved telephonic in-depth interviews (N = 19). Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive statistics, chi-square and McNemar's analysis (SPSS version 27.0), while reflexive thematic analysis was employed for qualitative data. Visual appeal of images was found to be significantly (p < 0.05) associated with willingness to consume the foods. Colour, visual effects, ingredients, and presentation were the factors determining the appeal and impact of food images on diet. The intervention primarily featured healthy food images (two-thirds of total), and a consistent positive trend was observed across attitudes, frequency of consumption and intention to consume. Norms commonly associated with unhealthy foods, such as higher purchase intentions and eating out with friends were more strongly associated with foodporn images of healthy foods than with regular images. Findings suggest that presenting healthy foods in a 'foodporn' way can positively incline adolescents towards healthier food choices. This strategy can be upscaled by fostering online communities that promote visually appealing, healthy food content.

abstract: Mobile health (mHealth) interventions show promise for supporting diabetic foot self-care; however, sustained engagement remains a challenge, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. While educational strategies are commonly used to address diabetic foot ulcers, they often fail to translate knowledge into long-term self-care. Understanding behavioral mechanisms underlying mHealth use, including the role of caregivers, is critical for improving implementation and effectiveness. This study explored how behavioral interactions between people with diabetes and caregivers shape the use of an mHealth app for diabetic foot self-care. This qualitative explanatory study was embedded within a parent study of an mHealth app for diabetic foot care that was conducted in primary care settings in Peru. It used the COM-B (capability, opportunity, motivation-behavior) model and the Theoretical Domains Framework (TDF) to identify mechanisms relevant for intervention design and scale-up. Semistructured interviews were conducted with people with diabetes and caregivers about their experiences related to accessing the app. Data were analyzed using deductive and inductive thematic analysis informed by the COM-B and TDF. In total, 14 people with diabetes (median age 54 y, 8 women and 6 men) and 10 caregivers (median age 28.5 y, all women) were interviewed. The app use depended on varying interactions between COM-B domains, while other behavioral determinants aligned with a single domain. Across domains, interactions between people with diabetes and caregivers also affected the app use. For example, caregivers often compensated for physical capability limitations through foot positioning or environmental adjustments. Environmental context and resources, including internet access, lighting, and device compatibility, affected the app use for all participants. Motivation for all participants was largely driven by beliefs about the app's preventive value, although reassurance from health professionals and altruism also emerged. The app use often depended on collaboration between people with diabetes and caregivers as a dyad, rather than on independent users. This highlights the need to design digital interventions around caregiver demographics, competing responsibilities, and the additional responsibilities an app may introduce. Participants' preference for individual follow-up suggests that nonphysician health personnel and other human support may help maintain continuity and reassurance alongside digital monitoring. Although the app was an early prototype intended for algorithmic training, participant experiences provided insight into real-world usability and contextual barriers for future app development.

abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic generated a notable emotional impact on the general population, yet its effects on incarcerated individuals have been far less explored, despite the particular vulnerabilities associated with prison environments. This study aimed to assess levels of anxiety and fear related to COVID-19 among incarcerated adults in Spain and identify sociodemographic and health-related factors associated with greater emotional distress. A cross-sectional study was conducted between May 2022 and February 2023 among 711 inmates from 3 Spanish prisons using a nonprobability convenience sampling strategy. Anxiety and fear related to COVID-19 were assessed using the Anxiety and Fear of COVID-19 Assessment Scale (AMICO)-Inmates scale, an adaptation of the original AMICO, developed for the general Spanish population, and subsequently validated for use among prison inmates. Descriptive analyses, bivariate comparisons, and categorical regression (CATREG) were performed to examine factors associated with the total AMICO score. The mean AMICO score was 5.58 (SD 2.55), indicating high levels of anxiety and fear related to COVID-19. In the bivariate analyses, significant differences were observed according to sex, having children, sharing a cell, and the presence of chronic illness. The CATREG model explained 17.4% of the variance in AMICO scores ( Incarcerated individuals experienced high levels of anxiety and fear related to COVID-19. Women, inmates sharing a cell, and those with chronic illnesses appeared particularly vulnerable to emotional distress. These findings highlight the importance of incorporating targeted psychological support and mental health strategies into prison preparedness plans for future public health emergencies.

abstract: To evaluate the impact of Family-Centered Care (FCC) practices on parental stress, anxiety, and depression among parents of children admitted to a Pediatric Intensive Care Unit (PICU). This prospective observational study was conducted over one year (September 2024-August 2025) in a PICU of a tertiary care teaching hospital in North India. Children aged 1 mo to 18 y admitted for more than 24 h were included. Parental psychological assessment was performed within 72 h of admission using the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) and the Parental Stressor Scale (PSS). FCC components-including information sharing, family participation, presence during procedures and resuscitation, family-centered rounds, dignity and respect, negotiating roles, sharing goals, family conferences, and open visitation-were documented. Illness severity was assessed using PRISM scores. Correlation and comparative analyses were performed to examine associations between FCC practices and psychological outcomes. A total of 326 children were enrolled. Higher PRISM scores correlated strongly with increased parental stress (r = 0.793), anxiety (r = 0.721), and depression (r = 0.719) (p <0.0001). Implementation of key FCC components was significantly associated with lower stress, anxiety, and depression scores (p <0.05). The number of FCC components followed showed a strong inverse correlation with stress (r = -0.836), anxiety (r = -0.709), and depression (r = - 0.754) (p <0.0001). Open visitation alone was not significantly associated with improved psychological outcomes. Structured FCC practices are significantly associated with reduced parental stress, anxiety, and depression in the PICU. Strengthening meaningful family engagement may improve psychological outcomes in resource-limited critical care settings.

abstract: Cooperation, as a mutual collaboration, is a defining feature of human social life. Individual characteristics can influence cooperation. Recent studies have shown a quadratic relationship between cardiac vagal tone (CVT), an index of self-regulation, and prosocial behaviors. Individual differences in cooperation might also vary as a function of people's environmental sensitivity (ES), i.e., may be influenced by individual differences in the perception and processing of inner and external stimuli. We tested the direct and interactive effect of CVT and ES on cooperative behaviors in two independent samples. We measured heart rate and engagement in cooperative acts in 80 young adults (M = 23.61; SD = 1.60) who were also asked to self-report on ES. We found an inverted-U relationship between CVT and cooperative behaviors. ES, on the other hand, did not predict differences in cooperative behaviors but moderated the relationships between CVT and cooperation, although the magnitude of this result was small. Specifically, only among individuals with higher ES cooperative behaviors change as a function of CVT. Highly sensitive individuals with lower or higher CVT, were less cooperative than low sensitive ones. Subsequently, we replicated the same study design in a second sample of 88 undergraduate students (M = 23.69; SD = 4.91). Once again, we found evidence supporting the presence of an inverted-U relationship between CVT and cooperative behaviors, and we also found that ES moderated the relationships between the quadratic CVT term and cooperation.

abstract: This study assessed the psychometric properties of the Dutch translation of the Prosocial Behavior Questionnaire (PBQ-NL), a self-report questionnaire that distinguishes altruistic, reactive, and proactive prosocial behaviours. Participants were 381 Dutch adolescents and young adults aged 13–30 (Mage = 18.62, SD = 2.59, 65.1% female). Test-retest reliability data were available for 199 participants. A Confirmatory Factor Analyses supported the three-factor structure of the questionnaire, with adequate six-month test-retest reliability. Altruistic and reactive prosocial behaviours correlated significantly and positively with prosocial behaviours directed at family/peers and the larger society, but not with depression or aggression. Conversely, proactively motivated prosocial behaviour correlated significantly and negatively with prosocial behaviour directed at family and positively with experienced opportunities for contribution to the larger society, aggression, and depression. These findings show that the PBQ-NL is a reliable measure to disentangle self- and other-serving motivations that underly prosociality during adolescence and young adulthood.

abstract: Personality prompts reshape how Large Language Models propose offers in economic games—but not how they respond to them. We show this by assigning graded Dark Factor of Personality profiles to 17 LLMs in the Ultimatum Game and benchmarking their decisions against human data. As proposers, LLMs shifted from 91% fair offers at the lowest selfishness level to 17% at the highest, closely tracking human patterns but with steeper gradients. As responders, no such shift occurred: acceptance rates remained uniformly high ( ∼ 80%) regardless of personality, failing to reproduce the punishment dynamics observed in humans. This asymmetry is theoretically informative. When incentive structures are explicit, personality and framing effects are attenuated—and proposing an offer is inherently more ambiguous than responding to one.. Most strikingly, personality prompts changed what responders articulated but not how they chose : model justifications showed systematic shifts in fairness language, yet behavioral output remained flat. This dissociation between stated reasoning and revealed behavior indicates that LLMs achieve linguistic compliance with personality prompts without corresponding motivational change—approximating human strategic behavior only where surface-level heuristics suffice.

abstract: To describe nursing staffs' perceptions of conducting suicide risk assessments via telephone within specialised psychiatric care. Twenty-two nursing staff working in three psychiatric care units in central Sweden were interviewed. Phenomenographic analysis was used to analyse the data. Technological advances now allow for multisensory assessments. As telephone communication lacks visual cues, nurses rely on mental imagery and intuition and listen to the patient's tone of voice. Suicide risk assessment demands collaboration and experience for collective validation. Together, these elements contribute to the creation of a safety net around the individual by the nursing staff. The study highlights a troubling shift towards standardised procedures at the expense of psychiatric competence, underscoring the need to preserve clinical expertise. Psychiatric nursing staff contributed to this study by sharing their experiences through interviews.

abstract: To explore stakeholder perspectives (including nurses, nursing supervisors, educators and parents) on the competencies perceived as important for providing paediatric end-of-life care. A qualitative design using semi-structured interviews and a conventional content analysis approach was employed. Data were collected through individual, in-depth, semi-structured face-to-face interviews. Multi-stakeholder purposive sampling with maximum variation was utilized. Audio-recorded interviews were transcribed verbatim and analysed using conventional qualitative content analysis following Graneheim and Lundman's approach. Data collection and iterative analysis proceeded until code saturation was achieved within the healthcare professional cohort. Primary qualitative data were collected between 1 April and 30 June 2025, across paediatric healthcare settings in the North of Iran (Rasht, Guilan). Data sources comprised 17 participants: 15 healthcare professionals (10 clinical paediatric nurses, 2 nursing supervisors and 3 nursing faculty members) and 2 bereaved parents whose children had received end-of-life palliative care. Data analysis revealed one overarching theme, 'Providing comprehensive and ethically oriented care for the child and family at the end of life', encompassing six stakeholder-identified competencies (main categories) and 17 subcategories. The six proposed categories were: (1) competencies in ethical and empathetic communication; (2) competencies in comprehensive physical care focused on the child's quality of life; (3) competencies in psychological care and bereavement support; (4) competencies in cultural and spiritual care; (5) ethical and advanced clinical decision-making competencies; and (6) competencies in interdisciplinary and team-based collaboration. From the perspective of key stakeholders, competent paediatric end-of-life nursing care extends beyond routine clinical skills, requiring comprehensive, ethically grounded and context-sensitive capabilities for supporting both the dying child and their family. These preliminary, stakeholder-informed competencies highlight the need for strengthening specialized educational curricula and supportive institutional infrastructure to enhance the quality of paediatric end-of-life care. Culturally responsive care: Highlights the need to incorporate cultural and spiritual coping strategies-such as faith in divine providence-into paediatric palliative care competencies, extending beyond Western-oriented frameworks. Navigating ethical tensions: Equips nurses to effectively navigate complex ethical dilemmas and facilitate family-centred decision-making in healthcare settings characterized by limited resources and prominent religious frameworks. Educational framework: Offers an evidence-based foundation for developing specialized undergraduate curricula, continuous professional development programs and clinical protocols for general nurses providing end-of-life care. This study addresses the lack of context-specific evidence on paediatric end-of-life nursing competencies in Iran. The findings clarify the professional competencies required to support dignified, high-quality end-of-life care, preserve children's dignity and empower families during decision-making and bereavement. These results are anticipated to inform nurses, educators and healthcare policymakers involved in paediatric palliative care. This study was reported in accordance with the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research (COREQ) checklist. Bereaved parents whose children passed away in paediatric units participated as key interviewees, contributing directly to qualitative data generation by sharing their lived experiences and expectations regarding nursing competencies during their child's end-of-life trajectory.

abstract: The fragmentation of sensitive medical data across institutions and stringent privacy regulations creates isolated data silos, hindering the development of robust AI-driven healthcare solutions. Existing approaches often lack sufficient trust mechanisms, comprehensive auditability, and dynamic access control for multi-center collaboration. Goal: This protocol aims to resolve the tension between collaborative utility and data sovereignty by integrating federated learning (FL) with blockchain technology, providing a secure, auditable, and scalable framework for medical data sharing. The framework employs a tripartite architecture: cryptographic FL with adaptive regularization and Paillier homomorphic encryption for privacy-preserving local training; a multi-channel, tiered-sharding blockchain for decoupled access control, data provenance, and FL operation logging; and a dynamic privacy-computation coordination mechanism that adapts differential privacy and cryptographic protocols based on data sensitivity and hardware capability. The workflow follows a sequential set of steps, including data preprocessing, local encrypted gradient generation, blockchain-backed secure aggregation, and global model updating. Under experimental conditions, the framework achieved 92.5% model accuracy after 20 training rounds and supported up to 30 nodes. No raw data exposure was detected, and tamper detection succeeded in all evaluated test cases. The architecture reduced computational overhead by 41% compared to a centralized baseline, achieved 96% automated regulatory compliance for audited access approvals, and demonstrated linear scalability, with the block generation interval stabilizing at 4.2 s.

abstract: Abstract This paper contributes to debates on problematic, dominant criminological narratives by foregrounding children’s own accounts of the support they need to thrive, informing ongoing efforts to support their individual and moral development. Drawing on community-based, participatory focus groups and individual and small-group interviews with 58 children aged 10–17 attending youth centres in Cambridge (UK), the study departs from deficit-oriented, adult-led explanations that frame children primarily through risk, mental disorders, or criminalisation. The findings rework prevailing criminological intervention approaches in two ways. First, using reflexive thematic analysis, the study centres children’s lived knowledge to identify trust, belonging, voice, agency, relational consistency of care, emotional support, and autonomy as central to what makes interventions trustworthy, accessible, engaging, and effective, whilst overly didactic, rigid, or authoritarian approaches were identified as key barriers to participation and effectiveness. These accounts move beyond adult assumptions about children’s needs, showing that effective support is grounded in relational, dialogic, autonomy-supportive environments rather than deficit-oriented models. Second, the paper argues that centring children’s perspectives is necessary but not sufficient: interventions must also be theoretically informed and evidence based. Rather than treating participatory and evidence-informed approaches as competing paradigms, the study offers data supporting their integration, combining child-centred qualitative insight with theoretically specified explanations of behaviour. Implications are discussed for the ongoing development of the school-based SATNAV:Compass youth intervention programme. This reconstruction of recommended intervention design approaches retains the strengths of existing traditions whilst addressing their limitations, offering a direction for future intervention research and practice.

abstract: Playful activities provide critical opportunities for rhythmic interactions, which may affect social and cognitive development in early childhood. Prior research suggests that motor synchrony promotes closeness and prosocial behaviour, but few studies have examined its role in social learning and in group settings. This study investigated whether motor synchrony in a clapping game, enhances preschoolers' closeness with others, imitation, over-imitation, and sharing behaviour. In a group setting, motor synchrony and asynchrony were experimentally induced between the child and two experimenters. We hypothesized that children would feel closer, imitate more, and share more with an adult partner who moved in synchrony compared to one who moved asynchronously. Bayesian analyses revealed no credible evidence that the children affiliated, imitated, over-imitated, or shared differently with their synchronous vs. asynchronous partner (BF10 = 0.045-0.216). Manipulation checks indicated that although the adults adhered to the stimuli, there was overall low motor synchrony. These findings highlight the challenges of inducing motor synchrony in playful group settings and raise questions about the level of synchrony necessary to impact social affiliation and learning in young children.

abstract: The book is divided into two parts. Part 1 (Chapters 1 and 2) lays the foundation for the rest of the work. It presents data on early access to media and institutional responses. It explores the meaning of incidental acquisition through cartoons. It offers an overview of effective experiences. Part 2 (Chapters 3–5) focuses on the analysis of children’s cartoons and a case study. The book aims to describe and provide evidence of early incidental second language acquisition through multi-year joyful exposure to cartoons. In so doing, the book attempts to reach a generalization of the process and the outcome, finally identifying the type of bilingualism that emerges. A review of key literature in cognitive psychology supports the hypothesis that this process mirrors certain aspects of first language acquisition. A co-viewing caregiver is underlined as a necessary condition. Animated cartoons are examined as multimodal resources that facilitate comprehension of a new language, while entertaining. Additionally, their formulaic and pragmatic language is analysed through scripts and prosodic features that play a central role in helping children acquire both fixed and flexible language patterns. Evidence of early second language acquisition is presented through global studies, with a particular focus on a qualitative analysis of a case study of two siblings.

abstract: Recently, reputation-based indirect reciprocity has been widely applied to the study on fairness behavior. Previous works mainly investigate indirect reciprocity by considering compulsory participation. While in reality, individuals may choose voluntary participation according to the opponent's reputation. It is still unclear how such reputation-based voluntary participation influences the evolution of fairness. To address this question, we introduce indirect reciprocity with voluntary participation into the dictator game (DG). We respectively consider good dictators or recipients can voluntarily participate in games when the opponents are assessed as bad. We theoretically calculate the fairness level under all social norms of third-order information. Our findings reveal that several social norms induce the high fairness level in both scenarios. However, more social norms lead to a high fairness level for voluntary participation of recipients, compared with the one of good dictators. The results also hold when the probability of voluntary participation is not low. Our results demonstrate that recipients’ voluntary participation is more effective in promoting the emergence of fairness behavior.

abstract: Brain health refers to the state of a person's brain function across various domains, including cognitive, behavioral and motor functions. Healthy brains are associated with better individual health, increased creativity, and enhanced productivity. A person's brain health is intricately connected to personal, social and environmental factors. Racial, ethnic, and social disparities affect brain health and on the global scale these disparities within and between regions present a hurdle to brain health. To overcome global disparities, greater collaboration between practitioners and healthcare providers and the people they serve is essential. This requires cultural humility driven by empathy. Empathy is a core prosocial value, a cognitive-emotional skill that helps us understand ourselves and others. This position paper aims to provide an overview of the vital roles of empathy, cooperation, and interdisciplinary partnerships. By consciously integrating this understanding in practice, leaders can better position themselves to address the diverse challenges faced by communities, promote inclusivity in policies and practices, and further more equitable solutions to the problem of global brain health.

abstract: This phenomenological qualitative study is an investigation of U.S. military-affiliated educators who teach senior military leaders people skills, such as self-awareness, emotional management, prosocial skills, and creativity, with the aim of enhancing military mission effectiveness by strengthening a leader's cognitive agility. The purpose of this study was to understand how educators experience the challenges and opportunities of translating people skills into practice, equipping leaders to manage stress, uncertainty, and decision-making demands in complex environments. Consequently, this study also addresses how educators ensure people skills are taught and implemented (or transferred) successfully within the target learner's organization. Traditionally, military executive training focused on operational or managerial grooming. Very few programs focused on people skills. However, the U.S. Armed Services are increasingly focusing on providing training to mitigate negative indicators among personnel and challenges in recruitment and retention. Thus, the focus of this study was on educators who provide these training protocols. The target audience for these protocols comprises senior military leaders. These veteran leaders present some educational challenges for instructors at the outset of training, such as overcoming a stigma associated with "softness," which might be perceived as weak in military culture, compounded by an "expertise" learner bias. The research addressed how these educators develop their lesson plans to meet the needs of military learners, the obstacles they face, and the strategies they employ to foster a productive learning environment. Findings from this study will contribute to a deeper understanding of the unique pedagogical challenges and opportunities in government-based military education programs.

abstract: The effects of beauty on judgment and behavior are well-established and somewhat "unidirectional" (i.e., it seems that only beautiful people reap social benefits). In particular, a person's beauty does not seem to have any effect on his/her own prosocial behavior. In the current research, we focus on how people relate themselves to beauty, namely beauty mindset, and how it may shape prosocial and altruistic behavior. We present 10 experiments (N = 4,449). Participants who hold a beauty growth-mindset (i.e., believing that beauty is improvable) donated more money to charity (vs. fixed-mindset), were more likely to get vaccinated against COVID-19 after exposure to an intervention focusing on herd-protection (vs. self-protection), and showed increased intention to engage in other forms of prosocial and altruistic behavior. Empirically, these effects are mediated by a self-perception of the ability to exert impact on others. abstract: Exercise testing is an established tool for assessing cardiorespiratory function, guiding management, and predicting outcomes in children, adolescents, and adults with congenital and/or paediatric acquired heart disease. Despite its widespread use, substantial variability exists among clinical paediatric exercise laboratories in testing protocols, calibration techniques, data interpretation, and reporting, limiting multicentre collaboration and data comparability. To describe the formation of a registry focused on pediatric exercise testing. The Pediatric Exercise Data Analytics and Learning Network was established in 2023 by six institutions as the first multicentre paediatric-focused exercise testing registry in the United States dedicated to patients with heart disease. The Pediatric Exercise Data Analytics and Learning Network has two primary actions: 1) develop and maintain a multicentre registry with uniform data definitions to support quality improvement and research; and 2) establish a learning network to advance education and knowledge sharing through standard operating procedures, benchmarking dashboards, and collaborative initiatives. Integration with Cardiac Networks United links the Pediatric Exercise Data Analytics and Learning Network's functional exercise testing data with existing longitudinal heart disease registries, creating opportunities for high-impact quality improvement and research. To foster objectives, the Pediatric Exercise Data Analytics and Learning Network aims to build a diverse network of both individual and hospital members who will work collaboratively to improve the consistency and value of paediatric and congenital exercise testing, advance quality improvement and research, and enhance long-term outcomes for patients with heart disease. This document describes the formation of PEDAL including organizational structure, database creation, and future directions.

abstract: Infant gut microbiota (IGM) development is shaped by multiple maternal, environmental, and feeding-related factors. Human milk contains microbial communities and bioactive components that may contribute to early microbial colonization and immune development. The aim of this study was to characterize paired human milk and IGM across early developmental time points and to examine their associations with allergic and allergy-related outcomes ascertained at the approximately 3-year follow-up. This retrospective cohort analysis included 60 mother-infant pairs, comprising 39 breastfed and 21 non-breastfed infants. At the approximately 3-year follow-up, children were classified into the allergy group (n=42) or non-allergy group (n=18) using the allergic/allergy-related history reported by parents at follow-up, including events with first onset after age 3 years. Infant fecal microbiota were evaluated in the eligible cohort, whereas human milk analyses were restricted to dyads with available milk samples. Microbiota at 1, 4, and 6 months were characterized by 16S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) gene sequencing, followed by diversity, differential-abundance, and correlation analyses. Exploratory analyses identified nominal between-group differences in the relative abundance of several taxa at individual time points; however, none of the taxon-level comparisons remained significant after false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Beta-diversity analysis of the IGM showed a nominal between-group difference at 1 month (Jaccard-based PERMANOVA, P=0.04), but not at 4 or 6 months. Linear discriminant analysis effect size (LEfSe) and correlation analyses suggested time-dependent microbial patterns that differed between the allergy and non-allergy groups, with the most prominent exploratory signals occurring early in infancy. These taxon-level findings should be regarded as hypothesis-generating. Exploratory differences in human milk and infant gut microbial communities were associated with allergic and allergy-related outcomes ascertained at the approximately 3-year follow-up. Because no taxon-level comparison remained significant after FDR correction, individual microbial signals should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory. Paired milk-gut patterns were consistent with potential maternal-infant microbial sharing, but strain-level transmission and causal relationships cannot be established by the present study design or 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Larger prospective studies with rigorous low-biomass controls, repeated-measures/compositional models, and strain-resolved functional analyses are needed.

abstract: Statewide immunization data are essential for monitoring vaccination trends and evaluating immunization program impact. In the United States, Immunization Information Systems (IIS) were established in the early 1990s to collect these data; however, operational, legal, and procedural details vary across states and over time. This study summarized differences in IIS characteristics, such as legal requirements and reporting procedures, across U.S. states and jurisdictions over time. We compiled jurisdiction-level IIS regulatory data from published studies and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) surveys conducted in 2000, 2012, 2018, and 2024 to compare changes in age-group coverage, provider reporting requirements, consent procedures, operating authority, and data-sharing regulations. Between 2000 and 2024, legal frameworks and reporting practices for immunization registries expanded across U.S. states and jurisdictions. The number of states with laws or administrative rules authorizing immunization registries increased from 24 states in 2000 to all 50 states, Washington, D·C., five metropolitan areas, five U.S. territories, and three Freely Associated States in 2024. Over the same period, reporting requirements also became more widespread. The number of states and jurisdictions mandating providers to report immunization records increased from 12 (24% of 51) in 2000 to 54 (84% of 64) in 2024. Consent policies also changed over time. By 2024, most states and jurisdictions had adopted implicit consent for reporting children's immunization records (41/64; 64%), while a smaller proportion required explicit parental consent (7/64, 11%) or implemented mandatory participation without consent (14/64, 22%). IIS infrastructure and reporting requirements have expanded across U.S. states and jurisdictions over the past two decades, while heterogeneity in consent policies and reporting practices persists. These temporal changes may need to be considered when interpreting IIS data, particularly in longitudinal and cross-jurisdictional analyses.

abstract: Germline genetic sequencing to detect cancer predisposition is increasingly used in pediatric oncology, yet little is known about families' experiences or their preferences regarding counseling, recontacting, and data sharing. This study explored these aspects among families of newly diagnosed children with cancer participating in a germline sequencing study. Parents of children with cancer of all ages (n = 335) and adolescents aged 12-18 years who were recently diagnosed with cancer (n = 49), who participated in a germline sequencing study at the national pediatric oncology center in the Netherlands, completed questionnaires about their experiences and counseling preferences. Sequencing included analysis of 142 cancer predisposition genes. Both adolescents and parents indicated that children should be involved in decisions about genetic testing, starting around the age of nine years. In this study, most children aged 11 years and older were actively involved. Counseling sessions with physician-researchers were reported as highly valued by both groups, especially compared with written consent forms. Notably, 80% of adolescents and 58% of parents reported that they had not fully read the written materials. Families showed no clear preference for supplementary information being paper, video, or web based. Regarding future recontacting, a large majority of parents (nearly 89%) agreed that hospitals should recontact families if new genetic insights arise, although most emphasized this should only occur with prior consent. Furthermore, nearly three-quarters of parents indicated that pediatric patients should provide their own consent for recontacting upon reaching adulthood. If asked personally, over 90% of parents would consent to being recontacted. Concerning data sharing, over 80% of parents supported sharing genetic data with other hospitals or research institutions for research purposes, but most felt this should require explicit consent and that children should reconsent at maturity. Parents reported prioritizing research that advances childhood cancer care and valued transparency about how data are used. Within this sample, families reported valuing early involvement of children, and direct engagement with healthcare professionals in counseling. Parents reported support for recontacting, reconsenting and international data sharing, provided that informed consent is maintained throughout childhood and into adulthood. These findings offer exploratory insights into family perspectives that may inform future research and the development of counseling approaches.

abstract: For nearly fifty years, federal corporate food waste legislation has consistently employed an aretaic (virtue-based) theoretical framework that assumes corporations will act as “Good Samaritans” when provided with appropriate incentives and liability protections. Beginning with Federal Tax Code Section 170(e)(3) in 1976 and continuing through the Bill Emerson Good Samaritan Food Donation Act (1996), the Federal Food Donation Act (2008), the Agri-cultural Improvement Act (2018), and the Food Donation Improvement Act (2022), United States policy has relied exclusively on voluntary compliance mechanisms rather than mandatory regulations. This Article argues that this approach is built on a myth, and that the myth operates on three interlocking levels. At the legislative level, it holds that corporations will donate surplus food if liability barriers are removed, a claim that fifty years of evidence has consistently refuted. At the hermeneutic level, it misreads the parable of the Good Samaritan itself: corporations in the food waste context are not the Samaritan, who acted voluntarily out of genuine compassion, but the innkeeper, who provided services in exchange for guaranteed payment. At the ideological level, it assumes that virtue can be cultivated in profit-driven entities whose fiduciary obligations run not to hungry communities but to shareholders. The consequences of this myth are measurable. Despite decades of tax incentives and liability shields, corporate food waste has increased from 30% of the available food supply in 1974 to nearly 40% today, while 47.4 million Americans experience food insecurity. Food waste in United States landfills generates 34% of all human-related methane emissions, substantially con-tributing to climate change that disproportionately harms the communities that food donation policies were designed to serve. The persistence of incidents like the 2021 Portland Fred Meyer controversy—where thousands of pounds of edible food were discarded and guarded from recovery by residents during a community crisis—demonstrates that voluntary approaches fail precisely when they are needed most. Even industry leaders fall short: after nine years of its Zero Hunger | Zero Waste initiative, Kroger, ranked first among United States supermarket chains for food waste commitment by the Center for Biological Diversity in 2019, only achieved a cumulative food waste reduction of less than 4% against a stated goal of 50% by 2025. This Article provides a comprehensive theoretical analysis of United States corporate food waste legislation, examining why virtue-based approaches have systematically failed to address the interconnected crises of food waste, food insecurity, and environmental harm. The analysis demonstrates that aretaic theory, which seeks to cultivate virtue through indirect encouragement rather than direct mandates, is fundamentally incompatible with corporate shareholder theory and profit-maximization imperatives. The Article further critiques France’s Garot Law, which mandates supermarket food donations through categorical duties, demonstrating that while this deontological approach achieved impressive increases in food donations, it failed to meaningfully reduce overall food insecurity due to its rigid, context-insensitive framework and the absence of monitoring capacity sufficient to ensure that donated food reached food-insecure communities. Moving beyond these existing approaches, this Article proposes a consequentialist-based Corporate Partner Food Waste Act, grounded in Congress’ Commerce Clause authority and administered by the EPA. Rather than assuming corporations will choose to do good, the Act would ensure they do good as a natural consequence of pursuing their interests within a well-designed system of mandatory requirements and measurable outcomes. The framework establishes food recovery requirements differentiated by geographic proximity to food-insecure communities—using USDA Food Access Research Atlas definitions as the baseline—creating “Priority Zones” and “Standard Zones” with distinct obligations tied to community need. Penalties are anchored to company revenue rather than fixed amounts, ensuring that the cost of non-compliance consistently exceeds the cost of compliance regardless of a company’s size. Annual performance reviews, comprehensive data collection, and an EPA Food Waste Reduction Coordinator provide the monitoring infrastructure that voluntary frameworks have consistently lacked. After five decades of legislative failure, this Article argues that the path forward requires abandoning the Good Samaritan myth entirely and replacing it with a regulatory framework that treats corporations not as potential virtuous actors, but as corporate partners whose obligations are enforceable, measurable, and calibrated to actual outcomes.

abstract: Introduction Since teachers play a pivotal role in students' well-being and school engagement, expecting to be rejected by a teacher based on a persons' background could have negative effects on affective and cognitive academic outcomes. This paper explores the hitherto understudied construct of students' background-based rejection expectation by teachers and school engagement. Method In a study with 7th grade students in Germany, we addressed the question of whether students' expectation of rejection by teachers is connected to their school engagement, grades, self-esteem, and academic self-concept. We explored which groups of students expect to be rejected, and we checked whether strong emotional teacher support can moderate the effect of rejection expectation on school engagement. Results A strong expectation of rejection is associated with lower emotional and behavioral school engagement, lower grades, self-esteem, and academic self-concept. Ethnic minority students and students with lower cultural capital expect rejection more than their peers. There is indication that a strong emotional teacher support could moderate the relationship between rejection expectation and minority students' emotional and cognitive school engagement. Discussion Expectation of rejection can be associated with several negative academic outcomes. More research is needed to better understand when and how students expect rejection. It is relevant to understand how schools can be culturally responsive and inclusive.

abstract: This study aimed to improve descriptive autism assessment for people with moderate to severe intellectual disabilities (ID) in the Netherlands. The goal was to co-design a framework including an overview of assessment instruments, and recommendations for evaluating broader functioning, for translating findings into daily care and for involving representatives and staff. We used a participatory design, involving parents/representatives, clinicians, care staff, and management from ID and mental health services. The process included a literature study of autism-related instruments, a Delphi study to reach consensus on suitable instruments, and four focus group discussions (FGDs) exploring stakeholder involvement and the role of assessment instruments in the diagnostic process. The literature study identified 20 relevant instruments, of which 13 were selected through the Delphi study (n=37, three rounds). Key selection criteria included low burden for individuals, use of multiple information sources, and strong psychometric quality. While quick assessments were preferred, concerns arose about oversimplifying the autism assessment. FGDs (n=5-12) highlighted eight themes on stakeholder involvement, focusing on timing, roles, and goals. Although no consensus emerged on an optimal combination of tools, clarity about an instrument's purpose and implications proved important. The final FGD identified five potentially overlapping phases in the diagnostic process. The co-designed framework provides an overview of instruments for the assessment of autism and emphasises early and continuous involvement of parents and caregivers. Their participation is essential for defining concerns, guiding assessment goals, sharing information, and applying diagnostic outcomes to improve daily care and support.

abstract: The paper proposes the Truth-Default Ingroup Hypothesis (TDIH), an evolutionary framework linking moral psychology, cumulative cultural learning, and online social polarization.Grounded in long-term empirical research on online public opinion and social data analysis, and drawing on evolutionary anthropology and theories of cumulative cultural learning, I examine how human moral emotions-originally evolved to promote cooperation and suppress deception-shape contemporary forms of online behavior such as flaming, outrage, misinformation, and social polarization.Building on this framework, I propose a novel theoretical model: the Truth-Default Ingroup Hypothesis (TDIH).This hypothesis argues that humans domesticated the deceptive potential of language by forming "truth-default ingroups" sustained by norms, reputation, and sanctions.These trust-based communities enabled cumulative learning but also fostered ingroup favoritism and parochial altruism.In digital society, the same evolved moral mechanisms-truth bias, conformity, and third-party punishment-are amplified by social media, producing moral outrage, polarization, and misinformation.Online flaming, hate speech, and "cancel culture" thus represent technologically intensified expressions of evolutionary cooperative instincts.Recognizing these evolutionary underpinnings allows sociology to reframe digital moral conflict not as a technological anomaly, but as an extension of humanity's deep moral architecture.

abstract: Introduction As a key indicator of positive interpersonal interaction, interpersonal synchrony is widely considered to be closely related to individuals’ cooperative behavior. However, the mechanisms through which interpersonal synchrony influences cooperation in real classroom contexts remain insufficiently explored. Based on perceived similarity theory, social identity theory, and the psychological process model explaining how synchrony promotes cooperation, this study examines the impact of interpersonal synchrony on perceived cooperation among high school students and tests the mediating roles of perceived similarity and ingroup identification. Methods A combination of experimental manipulation and questionnaire measures was employed. A music-accompanied synchrony paradigm was used to manipulate interpersonal synchrony, while perceived similarity, ingroup identification, and perceived cooperation were measured. A multi-wave longitudinal design was adopted to analyze both the immediate effects of synchrony activities on perceived cooperation and the persistence of these effects over time. Results The results indicate that synchronous movement enhances perceived similarity, ingroup identification, and classroom perceived cooperation. Perceived similarity and ingroup identification play a chain mediating role between synchrony activities and perceived cooperation in high school psychology classes. Discussion Interpersonal synchrony not only improves students’ perceived cooperation in the classroom but also operates through psychological mechanisms involving perceived similarity and ingroup identification, thereby deepening the understanding of the social functions of synchrony.

abstract: BACKGROUND: The experimental evaluation of young children's socio-emotional abilities is limited by the lack of existing specific measures to assess this population and by the relative difficulty for researchers to adapt measures designed for the general population. METHODS: This study examined six early social-emotional abilities in 86 typically developing children aged 1 to 3 years using an eye-tracking-based experimental paradigm that combined visual preference tasks adapted from pre-existing infant studies. OBJECTIVES: The aim of this study is to obtain developmental norms in six early social-emotional abilities in typical children aged 1 to 3 years that would be promising for an understanding of disorders of mental development. These developmental standards are essential to enable comparative assessments with children with atypical development, such as children with Profound Intellectual and Multiple Disabilities (PIMD). RESULTS: The participants had greater spontaneous visual preferences for biological (vs. non-biological) motion, socially salient (vs. non-social) stimuli, the eye (vs. mouth) area of emotional expressions, angry (vs. happy) faces, and objects of joint attention (vs. non-looked-at ones). Interestingly, although the prosocial (vs. antisocial) scene of the socio-moral task was preferred, both the helper and hinderer characters were equally gazed at. Finally, correlational analyses revealed that performance was neither related to participants' age nor to each other (dismissing the hypothesis of a common underpinning process). CONCLUSION: Our revised experimental paradigm is possible in infants aged 1 to 3 years and thus provides additional scientific proof on the direct assessment of these six socio-emotional abilities in this population.

abstract: Playful activities provide critical opportunities for rhythmic interactions, which may affect social and cognitive development in early childhood. Prior research suggests that motor synchrony promotes closeness and prosocial behaviour, but few studies have examined its role in social learning and in group settings. This study investigated whether motor synchrony in a clapping game, enhances preschoolers' closeness with others, imitation, over-imitation, and sharing behaviour. In a group setting, motor synchrony and asynchrony were experimentally induced between the child and two experimenters. We hypothesized that children would feel closer, imitate more, and share more with an adult partner who moved in synchrony compared to one who moved asynchronously. Bayesian analyses revealed no credible evidence that the children affiliated, imitated, over-imitated, or shared differently with their synchronous versus asynchronous partner (BF10=0.045-0.216). Manipulation checks indicated that although the adults adhered to the stimuli, there was overall low motor synchrony. These findings highlight the challenges of inducing motor synchrony in playful group settings and raise questions about the level of synchrony necessary to impact social affiliation and learning in young children.

abstract: School-aged children that experience social anxiety and have difficulty with interactions among peers can create significant challenges to their development in terms of both psychology and behavior. A team sport such as volleyball provides a common setting that naturally includes all aspects of social interaction (communication, cooperation, role coordination, etc.) and shared goals which is essential to improve the child's confidence in interacting socially and abilities to interact socially with peers. This research is an examination of the effect that a 12-week collective volleyball cooperative tactical training program will have on social anxiety and peer interaction in children (8-12). A sample of 80 healthy school-age children was obtained via two methods of campus based, voluntary and/or open recruitment. These children were then randomly assigned to either an experimental intervention group ( Group × Time Interaction Effects from a mixed-design ANOVA were found to be statistically significant for both of the outcomes (social anxiety and peer interaction) of this study. Children participating in an intervention that included an instructional program using the Collective Volleyball Cooperative Tactical Training Model showed significantly greater improvement than did those in the Control Condition in reducing their level of social anxiety as well as improving their peer interaction abilities over the course of the 12-weeks. Although we found a statistically-significant improvement in both children's social anxiety, and their peer interaction skills through a 12-week program, there is no data available for us to understand if those positive results will continue into the future because we did not assess children at later points in time. Thus, future researchers are encouraged to consider extended assessment periods as part of their study designs to determine how long such interventions have an impact. Secondly, as a feasibility study in a controlled environment showed promise for implementation of cooperative tactical volleyball programs, there may be barriers to successful implementation in regular school settings such as lack of facilities, class size and teacher workload. Future research is needed to examine how cooperative tactical volleyball programs can be adapted to encompass large groups of students and incorporated into routine physical education curriculum. Furthermore, although the intervention showed feasibility under controlled conditions, implementation in regular school settings may face practical challenges, including limited facilities, larger class sizes, and teacher workload. Future studies should examine how cooperative volleyball tactical training can be adapted for broader school-based implementation. Collective Volleyball Cooperative Tactical Training is an effective method for reducing social anxiety and improving the ability of school aged children to interact with peers. The program offers a viable, school-based model for integrating sport skills acquisition (training) and psychosocial growth through physical activity.
